To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Mindfulness-based interventions are more effective than no-treatment, but not in comparison with other active treatments.
MBIs are more effective than no intervention or treatment-as-usual but not in comparison with placebo or other active interventions.
mindfulness-based interventions (MBI) are effective for common mental disorders in the acute phase, but not in comparison with other treatments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of the efficacy of MBIs for common mental disorders.
the question of how mindfulness-based interventions (MBI) work in the treatment of common psychiatric disorders.
the empirical support for mindfulness meditation as treatment for common mental disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MBIs are more effective than no-treatment, but the effect size is small.
MBIs for CMD in the acute phase have weak empirical support.
the evidence-base of MBIs is not sufficiently strong to justify the wide-spread clinical implementation of MBIs for common mental disorders in the acute phase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a need to improve the methodological quality of future RCTs and that the evidence for the efficacy of MBI for CMDs in general and for specific disorders in particular is weak.
MBIs are not more effective than other active treatments for the acute phase of CMDs.
the evidence for MBIs for the treatment of CMDs is not strong.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evidence for MBIs is not as strong as often claimed.
MBIs should be tested in more rigorous RCTs and that more research is needed to understand what works for whom, under what conditions and why.
there is no empirical support for MBIs for common psychiatric disorders in the acute phase.
